scenario:
A company runs a three-tier web application across two AWS accounts within the same AWS Organization: a Shared Services account hosting a fleet of Network Load Balancers behind a central inspection VPC, and a Workload account hosting the application in a separate VPC. The security team requires that:

- Traffic from the Workload VPC to the Shared Services VPC must never traverse the public internet.
- The Shared Services team must be able to add or remove consuming accounts without modifying route tables in every workload VPC.
- The solution must scale to support hundreds of workload VPCs across many accounts in the future without hitting AWS's default VPC peering connection limits per VPC.

Which solution meets these requirements with the least ongoing operational overhead?

options.text: Create a VPC Peering connection between the Shared Services VPC and each Workload VPC. Update route tables in every VPC to route traffic to the peered CIDR ranges.
Create a Transit Gateway, attach every VPC (Shared Services and all Workload VPCs) to it, and configure Transit Gateway route tables to control which VPCs can reach the Shared Services VPC.
Deploy an AWS PrivateLink endpoint service in the Shared Services account fronted by the Network Load Balancers, and create VPC interface endpoints in each Workload VPC that consume the service.
Configure AWS Site-to-Site VPN connections between the Shared Services VPC and each Workload VPC using a Virtual Private Gateway.

explanation.correct: AWS PrivateLink is purpose-built for this exact pattern — a service provider (Shared Services, fronted by an NLB) exposing a service to many consumer VPCs/accounts without any VPC peering, route table changes, or CIDR overlap concerns. Adding a new consuming account is just a matter of accepting a new endpoint connection — the provider never touches route tables, and there's no limit tied to the number of consumers the way peering has a per-VPC peering connection soft limit (125 by default, though raisable). Traffic stays entirely on the AWS network backbone, never touching the public internet.

incorrect.A: VPC Peering doesn't scale here — peering is strictly 1:1 between VPCs, has no transitive routing, and each new workload VPC requires both a new peering connection AND route table updates in every VPC involved. This directly violates the "hundreds of VPCs" and "least operational overhead" requirements.
incorrect.B: A very plausible-looking distractor, and often the right answer for full network-layer connectivity between many VPCs — but it's the wrong tool here because it grants full network reachability (not just access to specific NLB-fronted services), and still requires the Shared Services team to manage Transit Gateway route table associations/propagations for every new attachment. PrivateLink better matches "expose one service, don't manage per-consumer routing."
incorrect.D: Site-to-Site VPN is designed for connecting to on-premises networks, not VPC-to-VPC connectivity within AWS. It adds unnecessary encryption/tunnel overhead and per-connection management, with no advantage over PrivateLink or Transit Gateway for intra-AWS traffic.

scenario:
A central platform team manages networking for a large enterprise with 40 application teams, each operating its own AWS account under the same AWS Organization. Requirements:

- All application teams should deploy resources into a shared pool of subnets managed centrally, to avoid IP address exhaustion and inconsistent CIDR planning across 40 separate VPCs.
- Application teams must be able to launch EC2 instances, RDS databases, and other resources into these shared subnets from their own accounts.
- Application teams must NOT be able to modify the shared VPC's route tables, security group defaults, or subnet configuration — only the central platform team should control those.
- The solution should minimize the number of VPCs, cross-VPC connections, and peering relationships the platform team has to manage.

Which approach satisfies these requirements?

options.text: Create a VPC per application team, and use AWS Transit Gateway to connect all 40 VPCs together with a shared services VPC containing common resources.

Use VPC sharing (via AWS Resource Access Manager) to share subnets from a single central VPC owned by the platform team's account with each of the 40 application team accounts as participants, allowing each team to launch resources into the shared subnets while the platform team retains ownership of the VPC, route tables, and NACLs.
Create a VPC per application team and use VPC peering between each application team's VPC and a shared services VPC to centralize IP address management.
Grant each application team's IAM role a resource-based policy to create resources directly inside the platform team's VPC, and rely on IAM policies alone to prevent route table modification.

explanation.correct: VPC sharing (RAM-shared subnets) is the exact AWS feature for this scenario: a single owner VPC's subnets are shared with participant accounts, which can launch resources (EC2, RDS, etc.) into those subnets using their own account's billing and resource ownership — but participants can never modify the VPC's route tables, NACLs, security group defaults, gateways, or peering/attachment configuration, since only the owning account controls those. This collapses 40 potential VPCs into one, directly minimizing CIDR planning overhead and eliminating the need for any peering or Transit Gateway attachments between teams.

incorrect.A: 40 separate VPCs plus a Transit Gateway still means 40 CIDR ranges to plan and 40 attachments to manage — it doesn't minimize VPC count or avoid CIDR exhaustion planning. Each team also still fully owns and can modify its own VPC's route tables, which fails the "must not modify" requirement.
incorrect.C: Full mesh-style peering to a shared services VPC still requires 40 separate VPCs and up to 40 peering connections, directly contradicting the "minimize VPCs and connections" requirement, and again each team retains full control over its own VPC.
incorrect.D: IAM resource-based policies aren't how cross-account subnet access is granted in AWS — VPC sharing via RAM is the actual mechanism. Relying on IAM policies alone to prevent infrastructure changes is weaker and not how AWS implements this boundary.

scenario:
A global company has 10 VPCs in us-east-1 and 8 VPCs in eu-west-1, plus an on-premises data center connected via Direct Connect to us-east-1. Requirements:

- All VPCs within each Region must be able to communicate with each other and with the on-premises network.
- Three specific VPCs in us-east-1 hold PCI workloads (the "Sensitive" segment) and must NOT be reachable from any eu-west-1 VPC, even though all VPCs will attach to Transit Gateways.
- Cross-Region traffic between the two Regions' Transit Gateways must never traverse the public internet.

Which combination of actions meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a single Transit Gateway in us-east-1, attach the eu-west-1 VPCs to it via VPC peering, and use one Transit Gateway route table for all attachments.

Create a Transit Gateway in each Region, connect them with Transit Gateway peering, and use multiple Transit Gateway route tables per Region — associating the Sensitive VPC attachments with a dedicated route table that does not have routes propagated to or from the eu-west-1 attachments.
Create a Transit Gateway in each Region, connect them with a Site-to-Site VPN over the internet, and rely on Security Groups alone in the Sensitive VPCs to block traffic from eu-west-1.
Create separate VPC peering connections between every pair of VPCs across both Regions and use NACLs to block traffic from eu-west-1 into the Sensitive VPCs.

explanation.correct: Transit Gateway peering connects two regional Transit Gateways privately over the AWS backbone, satisfying "never traverse the public internet." Network segmentation is achieved with multiple Transit Gateway route tables: associating the Sensitive VPCs' attachments with a route table that doesn't propagate routes to/from the eu-west-1 attachments isolates them at the routing layer, while all other same-Region VPCs and the on-premises network continue to communicate normally through their own associated/propagated route tables. This is the standard Transit Gateway network-segmentation pattern.

incorrect.A: Transit Gateway doesn't span Regions this way — cross-Region connectivity requires Transit Gateway peering between two regional Transit Gateways, not plain VPC peering directly to a Transit Gateway. A single shared route table also provides no segmentation at all.
incorrect.C: A Site-to-Site VPN over the internet directly violates the "must never traverse the public internet" requirement. Security Groups alone also don't provide network-level route isolation — they filter traffic to/from resources that are still routable, which is a weaker and less reliable segmentation boundary than route table isolation.
incorrect.D: A full mesh of VPC peering connections across 18 VPCs doesn't scale (no transitive routing, and a rapidly growing number of pairwise connections to manage), and NACLs are a much higher-maintenance, per-subnet mechanism compared to centralized route-table-based segmentation at the Transit Gateway.

scenario:
A financial services company has a single AWS Direct Connect connection from its data center to a Direct Connect location, terminating in a private VIF on a Virtual Private Gateway. Requirements:

- Loss of any single Direct Connect location or device must not cause a full connectivity outage.
- The design should follow an AWS-documented resiliency model that eliminates single points of failure in the Direct Connect path.
- If all Direct Connect paths fail simultaneously, traffic must automatically fail over to an encrypted path over the internet, with no manual intervention required.

Which combination of steps satisfies these requirements?

options.text: Provision a second Direct Connect connection at the same Direct Connect location, using the same device and cross-connect, and configure equal BGP priority on both.

Following the AWS Direct Connect Resiliency Toolkit, provision two Direct Connect connections at two different Direct Connect locations terminating on different devices, and configure a Site-to-Site VPN as a backup path with a less-preferred BGP path (e.g. longer AS_PATH) than the Direct Connect routes.
Use a single Direct Connect connection with a Link Aggregation Group (LAG) to increase throughput, and rely on Direct Connect's built-in automatic failover to the internet.

Provision two Direct Connect connections at two different Direct Connect locations behind a Direct Connect Gateway and Transit Gateway, and omit a VPN backup since the Direct Connect Gateway is redundant by default.

explanation.correct: The Direct Connect Resiliency Toolkit's "High Resiliency" model (and above) requires connections at multiple Direct Connect locations terminating on separate devices, eliminating both location- and device-level single points of failure. Layering a Site-to-Site VPN backup path with a deliberately less-preferred BGP route (longer AS_PATH or lower local preference relative to the Direct Connect routes) means BGP will naturally prefer Direct Connect when available and automatically fail over to the encrypted VPN path if all Direct Connect routes are withdrawn — with no manual re-routing needed.

incorrect.A: Using the same location and device provides no protection against a location- or device-level failure — both connections share the same failure domain, which the Resiliency Toolkit explicitly guards against.
incorrect.C: Direct Connect has no built-in automatic failover to the internet — a VPN or a second Direct Connect connection must be explicitly provisioned and configured as backup. LAG only aggregates bandwidth and redundancy of links to the same location, not against a location-level outage.
incorrect.D: A Direct Connect Gateway is a routing construct for connecting Direct Connect connections to VPCs across regions/accounts — it does not itself provide a backup connectivity path. Omitting the VPN backup leaves no failover option if both Direct Connect connections fail at once (e.g., a regional Direct Connect service disruption), violating the automatic-internet-failover requirement.

scenario: A company connects an on-premises data center to a VPC using a single AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection (two tunnels, active/standby). The on-premises-to-AWS application needs sustained throughput of 3 Gbps, but each VPN tunnel is capped at roughly 1.25 Gbps. The company also wants the design to scale to connect dozens of on-premises sites to hundreds of VPCs in the future without significant added operational complexity, and cannot provision Direct Connect due to a short project timeline. What should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Increase the customer gateway device to a larger EC2 instance type to raise the per-tunnel throughput beyond 1.25 Gbps.

Provision multiple Site-to-Site VPN connections to a Transit Gateway and enable Equal Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) routing across the tunnels to aggregate bandwidth, using the Transit Gateway as the hub for future on-premises sites and VPCs.
Replace the Site-to-Site VPN with a single AWS Client VPN endpoint, which supports higher per-connection throughput than Site-to-Site VPN.
Enable Accelerated Site-to-Site VPN on the existing single VPN connection terminating on a Virtual Private Gateway, which removes the per-tunnel throughput cap entirely.

explanation.correct: The ~1.25 Gbps per-tunnel limit is a protocol-level IPsec constraint, not something a larger customer gateway instance can overcome. AWS's documented pattern for exceeding a single tunnel's throughput is multiple VPN connections combined with ECMP routing through a Transit Gateway, which can spread traffic across several tunnels to aggregate bandwidth. A Transit Gateway also naturally scales into a hub-and-spoke model for connecting many future sites and VPCs with minimal added operational complexity.

incorrect.A: The per-tunnel throughput cap is a fixed protocol-level limit of the IPsec tunnel itself, not a function of the customer gateway device's compute size — a larger instance won't raise it.
incorrect.C: AWS Client VPN is designed for individual remote user/device access (an OpenVPN-based solution), not site-to-site network connectivity, and isn't a throughput-superior substitute for this use case.
incorrect.D: Accelerated Site-to-Site VPN uses AWS Global Accelerator to improve routing and connection reliability to the nearest AWS edge location — it does not remove or raise the ~1.25 Gbps per-tunnel throughput cap. Multiple tunnels with ECMP are still required to scale aggregate throughput.

scenario:
A media company runs an application in two AWS Regions (us-east-1 primary, ap-southeast-1 secondary) behind an Application Load Balancer in each Region. Requirements:

- Under normal conditions, users should be routed to whichever Region gives them the lowest network latency.
- If the primary Region's ALB becomes unhealthy, traffic must automatically fail over to the secondary Region, without depending on individual clients' DNS caching behavior to eventually pick up the change.
- The company is also running a canary release in us-east-1 and wants only 5% of us-east-1-directed traffic to reach the canary environment, with the rest going to the stable environment — without altering the latency-based/failover behavior between the two Regions.

How should a solutions architect design the Route 53 record set to satisfy all of these requirements?

options.text: Create two simple A records, one per Region, and have the application redirect canary traffic client-side.

Create latency-based alias records for us-east-1 and ap-southeast-1, each with an associated Route 53 health check so an unhealthy Region is automatically excluded from DNS answers. Under the us-east-1 latency record, use a nested weighted record set (95%/5%) as the alias target to split traffic between the stable and canary target groups.
Create a single weighted record set with the two Regions weighted 50/50, attach a health check to each weighted record, and manually adjust the weights during each canary release to redirect traffic.
Create a failover routing policy with us-east-1 as primary and ap-southeast-1 as secondary, and use a separate CNAME for canary traffic that customers must opt into manually.

explanation.correct: This requires nesting Route 53 routing policies, an advanced but well-documented pattern: a latency-based record set with health checks determines the lowest-latency healthy Region and lets Route 53 itself exclude an unhealthy Region's answers at the authoritative DNS level (rather than depending on client-side caching behavior). Nesting a weighted record set specifically under the us-east-1 latency-based record then splits only that Region's traffic 95/5 between stable and canary, without touching ap-southeast-1's routing at all.

incorrect.A: Simple records provide no latency-based or health-check-driven failover behavior — this fails both the latency-routing and automatic-failover requirements outright.
incorrect.C: A flat 50/50 weighted policy doesn't route by latency (violating the first requirement), and manually adjusting weights for every canary release is exactly the kind of operational overhead a well-architected design should avoid, not require.
incorrect.D: A failover policy satisfies automatic Region failover but abandons latency-based routing entirely under normal conditions (violating the first requirement), and a manual opt-in CNAME doesn't deliver the required automatic 5% canary split.

scenario:
A software company (Provider Co.) wants to offer its internal analytics API as a paid service to external customers, each operating an independent AWS account outside Provider Co.'s AWS Organization. Requirements:

- Customers must reach the API privately from their own VPCs, without traversing the public internet, and Provider Co. must have no visibility into or control over customers' networks.
- Provider Co. must be able to explicitly approve or reject each customer's connection request before it becomes active.
- Customers should reach the API using a friendly, private DNS name (e.g. api.providerco.com) rather than an AWS-generated endpoint DNS name.
- Provider Co.'s infrastructure details (VPC CIDR, instance IPs, etc.) must remain hidden from customers at all times.

Which solution meets all of these requirements?

options.text: Provider Co. creates a VPC peering connection with each customer's VPC and shares route tables so customers can access the API using Provider Co.'s private IP addresses directly.

Provider Co. creates an AWS PrivateLink endpoint service backed by a Network Load Balancer in front of the API, requires manual acceptance for new endpoint connections, and associates a verified private DNS name so customers can resolve api.providerco.com to the interface endpoint inside their own VPC.

Provider Co. publishes the API through a public Amazon API Gateway endpoint secured with API keys, and instructs customers to allow-list Provider Co.'s IP ranges in their own VPC's outbound security group rules.
Provider Co. creates a Transit Gateway and shares it with each customer account via AWS Resource Access Manager, and each customer attaches their VPC to Provider Co.'s Transit Gateway.

explanation.correct: AWS PrivateLink is purpose-built for exactly this cross-organization SaaS-provider pattern: it exposes only the NLB's listening ports to consumers, hiding the provider's VPC CIDR, route tables, and instance IPs entirely; it requires explicit connection acceptance so the provider approves each customer individually; and it supports a verified private DNS name for the endpoint service so customers can use a custom domain instead of the auto-generated vpce-*.amazonaws.com name — all without the provider touching any customer network configuration.

incorrect.A: VPC Peering exposes full network reachability and requires sharing/coordinating route tables between two independent organizations, directly violating "infrastructure details must remain hidden," and it has no per-connection approval workflow at the granularity PrivateLink provides.
incorrect.C: A public API Gateway endpoint traverses the public internet, violating that explicit requirement, and IP allow-listing is brittle and doesn't scale cleanly across many independent customer accounts compared to a private, connection-based network solution.
incorrect.D: Sharing a Transit Gateway via RAM grants full network-layer reachability into all of Provider Co.'s TGW-attached VPCs to any account that attaches — the opposite of hiding infrastructure — and it isn't designed for onboarding untrusted third-party accounts the way PrivateLink's explicit accept/reject model is.

scenario: A company wants to delegate to its DevOps team the ability to create new IAM roles and policies for their applications, but must guarantee that no one — including the DevOps team itself, even by accident — can ever create or escalate a role to administrator-level access. Developers still need to be able to create functional roles for legitimate application services. Which approach achieves this?

options.text: Attach an explicit Deny policy to each DevOps IAM user for iam:CreateRole with a condition matching the AdministratorAccess managed policy ARN.

Set a permissions boundary on the DevOps IAM role that caps the maximum permissions any role or user the DevOps team creates can ever have, and grant DevOps iam:CreateRole/iam:PutRolePolicy permissions only when that boundary is specified.
Use an AWS Config rule to detect any IAM role that has AdministratorAccess attached and automatically delete it on a scheduled basis.
Create a Service Control Policy at the OU level that denies iam:CreateRole entirely, and grant DevOps engineers break-glass root access whenever they need to create a new role.

explanation.correct: Permissions boundaries are IAM's mechanism for capping the maximum permissions a delegated administrator (here, DevOps) can ever grant to identities they create. Even if DevOps attaches an overly broad policy to a new role, the role's effective permissions are the intersection of its policy AND the boundary — so it can never exceed the boundary, regardless of what DevOps grants. This lets DevOps keep creating functional roles for legitimate services while making privilege escalation architecturally impossible rather than merely policy-forbidden.

incorrect.A: An explicit deny targeting one specific managed policy ARN is trivially bypassed — DevOps could attach an inline policy or a different managed policy with equivalent permissions. It blocks one technique, not the underlying capability.
incorrect.C: Detect-and-delete is a reactive, not preventive, control — there's a window where an over-privileged role exists and could already have been used before Config catches and removes it. This fails "guarantee...can ever," which requires prevention.
incorrect.D: Denying iam:CreateRole entirely via SCP blocks DevOps from creating any role at all, including legitimate ones for application services — violating the requirement that developers must still be able to create functional roles. Routine break-glass root access is also a security anti-pattern and heavy operational overhead.

scenario:
A company acquires another company and must bring the acquired company's 15 existing standalone AWS accounts into its AWS Organization. Requirements:

- Consolidated billing must cover all accounts, including the newly acquired ones.
- The acquiring company's existing SCP guardrails must eventually apply to the acquired accounts, but NOT immediately — there needs to be a grace period while each acquired account's workloads are assessed for compliance.
- The acquired accounts' workloads must keep running without service interruption throughout the process.

Which approach satisfies these requirements?

options.text: Have the acquired company close all 15 existing accounts and create brand-new accounts inside the acquiring company's AWS Organization, manually migrating all resources.

Send an invitation from the Organization's management account to each of the 15 existing accounts to join the Organization; place newly joined accounts into a dedicated, temporary OU with no (or minimal) SCPs attached, then move each account into the appropriate production OU with full SCPs once its assessment is complete.
Use AWS Control Tower's Account Factory to enroll the 15 existing accounts, which immediately and unconditionally attaches all guardrails currently applied to other accounts.
Add the 15 accounts to the Organization directly under the root, and rely on IAM policies within each account to temporarily block actions until the account is assessed.

explanation.correct: AWS Organizations lets existing standalone accounts be invited to join an Organization without recreating them or interrupting running workloads. Placing newly invited accounts into a dedicated staging/quarantine OU with no or minimal SCPs — since SCPs are inherited by OU membership — then moving them into production OUs (with full guardrails) once assessed is the standard "safe landing zone for acquired accounts" pattern, cleanly satisfying the grace-period requirement. Consolidated billing applies automatically to every member account the moment it joins, satisfying that requirement immediately.

incorrect.A: Recreating accounts and manually migrating every resource is extremely high-effort, causes service interruption, and is exactly what the account-invitation feature of Organizations exists to avoid.
incorrect.C: Control Tower enrollment of existing accounts does apply guardrails, but doing so "immediately and unconditionally" directly contradicts the explicit grace-period requirement before enforcement.
incorrect.D: SCPs are the correct org-level control for this, not per-account IAM policies — IAM policies can't provide the same organization-wide guardrail enforcement, and manually rigging temporary IAM blocks across 15 separate accounts is far higher operational overhead than simple OU placement.

scenario: A security team wants to guarantee that no IAM principal in any account within a specific OU (containing all production accounts) can ever disable AWS CloudTrail, delete CloudTrail logs, or disable GuardDuty — including the account's own root user or an administrator holding an AdministratorAccess IAM policy. Which approach achieves this guarantee?

options.text: Attach an IAM policy to every administrator role in each production account explicitly denying cloudtrail:StopLogging, cloudtrail:DeleteTrail, and guardduty:DeleteDetector.

Attach a Service Control Policy to the production OU that explicitly denies cloudtrail:StopLogging, cloudtrail:DeleteTrail, and guardduty:DeleteDetector, and ensure no SCP elsewhere in the hierarchy re-allows them.
Enable an AWS Config managed rule that flags CloudTrail or GuardDuty being disabled, and send an SNS notification to the security team when this happens.
Use IAM Access Analyzer to continuously monitor and automatically revoke any permissions related to CloudTrail or GuardDuty modification across all production accounts.

explanation.correct: SCPs are the only control here that applies to every principal in an account — including the root user — and they set a hard ceiling that no IAM policy within the account can ever exceed, no matter how privileged. This is the only option that can guarantee the action is blocked "even for the root user," since IAM policies don't restrict root the same way, and detective controls only report on an action after it has already happened.

incorrect.A: IAM policies attached to administrator roles don't apply to the account's root user, and a sufficiently privileged administrator could simply detach or modify the policy itself — IAM policies aren't a hard ceiling the way SCPs are, so this isn't a guarantee.
incorrect.C: Config plus SNS is a detective control: it tells the security team AFTER CloudTrail or GuardDuty has already been disabled, not a preventive guarantee that it never happens.
incorrect.D: IAM Access Analyzer identifies external/unintended access and unused permissions for review — it doesn't proactively revoke permissions in real time to block specific API calls; this describes a capability Access Analyzer doesn't have.

scenario:
A company is building a brand-new multi-account AWS environment from scratch for a 200-person engineering organization expected to grow past 500 accounts within three years. Requirements:

- Consistent security and compliance guardrails must be automatically applied to every new account from the moment it's created.
- Engineering teams need self-service account provisioning, without the central platform team manually creating each account.
- Centralized visibility into guardrail compliance status is required across all accounts.
- The platform team is only 3 people, so initial setup effort must be minimized.

Which approach best meets these requirements?

options.text: Manually create each AWS account using AWS Organizations, write custom CloudFormation StackSets to deploy baseline security resources to each account, and build an internal ticketing system for account requests.

Use AWS Control Tower to set up a landing zone with preventive (SCP-based) and detective (Config-based) guardrails, and let engineering teams self-service provision new accounts through the Account Factory, each automatically inheriting the landing zone's guardrails.
Create one large shared AWS account for all 500 engineers and use IAM policies alone to separate teams, avoiding multi-account management entirely.
Use AWS Organizations with SCPs only, and let each engineering team independently create and configure their own accounts outside any centralized governance model, retrofitting guardrails later.

explanation.correct: This is exactly what Control Tower automates: landing zone setup (Organizations plus logging/audit accounts and guardrails) with minimal manual effort for a small platform team, self-service account provisioning via Account Factory so engineering teams don't wait on the platform team, automatic application of both preventive and detective guardrails to every new account, and centralized compliance visibility through the Control Tower dashboard — satisfying every stated requirement with the least initial setup effort.

incorrect.A: Hand-building StackSets and a ticketing system for account provisioning is a large custom-engineering burden for a 3-person team — the opposite of minimizing setup effort — and doesn't give the automatic new-account guardrail application Control Tower provides out of the box.
incorrect.C: A single shared account for 500 engineers fails basic security isolation and blast-radius principles the exam consistently tests against; IAM policies alone can't replicate the isolation a multi-account strategy provides.
incorrect.D: Retrofitting guardrails after account creation, rather than applying them automatically at creation time, leaves a window of ungoverned accounts and requires ongoing manual remediation — directly contradicting "automatically applied... from the moment it's created."

scenario:
A healthcare company stores PHI in S3 buckets across multiple AWS accounts (encrypted with SSE-KMS) within the same AWS Organization. Requirements:

- A single Security account should own and manage the KMS keys used to encrypt PHI data, for centralized key management and audit.
- Application accounts must be able to use these keys to encrypt/decrypt their own S3 data, without being able to modify the key policy, delete the key, or grant other accounts access to it.
- Every key usage — every encrypt/decrypt call, by whom, from which account — must be centrally auditable.
- If a key is ever compromised or needs replacing, existing encrypted data must remain decryptable without re-encrypting the entire multi-petabyte dataset.

Which combination of actions meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a separate customer managed KMS key in each application account, and use S3 Cross-Region Replication to centralize copies of all objects in the Security account for auditing.

Create customer managed KMS keys in the Security account with a key policy that grants specific application accounts kms:Encrypt/kms:Decrypt/kms:GenerateDataKey (but not kms:PutKeyPolicy or kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion), reference the key by ARN in each application account's S3 default encryption setting, enable automatic key rotation, and rely on AWS CloudTrail (which logs all KMS API calls) for centralized auditing.
Use the AWS-managed key (aws/s3) in each application account, since AWS-managed keys already provide automatic centralized management with no configuration needed.
Create one customer managed KMS key in the Security account and share the raw key material with each application account so they can perform encryption locally without calling the KMS API each time.

explanation.correct: A KMS key policy is the primary cross-account access-control mechanism for a key: granting specific actions (Encrypt/Decrypt/GenerateDataKey) to application account principals while withholding key-management actions (PutKeyPolicy, ScheduleKeyDeletion, CreateGrant) achieves centralized ownership with least-privilege cross-account usage. Every KMS API call is automatically logged to CloudTrail with the calling account and identity, satisfying centralized auditability. KMS's automatic annual key rotation replaces only the backing cryptographic material while keeping the same key ID/ARN, so previously encrypted data stays decryptable without any re-encryption — directly satisfying the compromised-key requirement.

incorrect.A: Separate keys per account plus S3 replication for "auditing" doesn't centralize key management at all (violating the core requirement) and needlessly duplicates a multi-petabyte dataset just to inspect access patterns — CloudTrail already provides this without replication.
incorrect.C: AWS-managed keys (aws/s3) cannot be shared across accounts via a custom key policy — they're scoped to a single account/service and don't support the cross-account access-control model this scenario requires, nor the fine-grained "can't delete/modify policy" separation, since there's no custom key policy to write.
incorrect.D: KMS key material is never exportable or shareable by design — that's the core security guarantee of the service, backed by HSMs. This option describes something KMS fundamentally does not support.

scenario:
A managed-service provider (MSP) manages AWS infrastructure for 50 client companies, each with its own separate AWS account (none inside the MSP's AWS Organization). MSP engineers need to operate in any client account. Requirements:

- MSP engineers must never have long-lived IAM credentials (access keys) stored in or issued for client accounts.
- Each client must be able to independently revoke the MSP's access at any time, without depending on the MSP's cooperation.
- Access granted to the MSP must be scoped to only what's needed (least privilege), and different clients may want to authorize different permission sets.
- The MSP must never be able to grant itself broader access than what each client explicitly authorized.

Which approach satisfies these requirements?

options.text: Each client creates an IAM user for the MSP with an access key and shares the credentials over a secure channel; the MSP stores these credentials in its own secrets manager.

Each client creates an IAM role with a trust policy allowing the MSP's AWS account to assume it (optionally requiring an external ID), attaches a permissions policy scoped to only what that client authorizes, and MSP engineers use AWS STS AssumeRole from their own IAM identities to obtain temporary credentials scoped to that role whenever needed.
The MSP creates a single IAM role in its own account with AdministratorAccess and shares that role's credentials with all client accounts to simplify management.
Each client adds the MSP's AWS account as a member of their AWS Organization and applies an SCP granting the MSP account full access to all resources.

explanation.correct: Cross-account IAM roles with AssumeRole are AWS's recommended pattern for third-party/MSP access: STS issues only short-lived temporary credentials on each assumption, so no long-lived credentials are ever created or shared. The client fully owns the role and its trust policy, so access can be revoked instantly (by deleting or updating the role) without the MSP's involvement. The client also defines the role's permissions policy, so each client can scope different permissions, and the MSP can never grant itself more than that policy allows since the client — not the MSP — controls it. An external ID in the trust policy additionally mitigates the confused-deputy problem when one MSP account is trusted by many clients.

incorrect.A: Long-lived IAM access keys directly violate "must never have long-lived credentials," are harder to revoke instantly compared to updating a role's trust policy, and carry ongoing credential-leakage risk.
incorrect.C: A single AdministratorAccess role fully controlled by the MSP violates least privilege and "must never grant itself broader access than authorized" — the MSP, not each client, would control the permissions, and every client would receive identical, excessive access.
incorrect.D: Making the MSP a full member of each client's Organization with a broad SCP is both operationally extreme and gives the MSP far more integration and visibility into the client's environment than a scoped cross-account role requires. SCPs also don't function as a mechanism to grant access to an external account this way — they set maximum permissions within an Organization, not cross-account grants.

scenario: An e-commerce company's order-processing system currently uses nightly cross-region backups, giving an RTO of several hours and an RPO of about 24 hours. A new business requirement mandates an RTO under 15 minutes and an RPO under 1 minute. However, the company explicitly wants to avoid the cost of running full production capacity simultaneously in two Regions. Which disaster recovery strategy should they adopt?

options.text: Continue with Backup and Restore, simply taking backups every hour instead of nightly.
Adopt Pilot Light: keep only the database continuously replicating in the DR Region, provisioning application servers from scratch during failover.
Adopt Warm Standby: run a scaled-down but fully functional copy of the entire application stack in the DR Region at all times, scaling it up on failover.
Adopt Multi-Site Active/Active: run full production capacity in both Regions simultaneously, actively serving traffic from both.

explanation.correct: Warm Standby's typical RTO (minutes) and RPO (seconds) both comfortably satisfy the sub-15-minute/sub-1-minute targets, and unlike Multi-Site Active/Active it only requires a scaled-down copy running continuously rather than full duplicate production capacity — satisfying the stated cost constraint as well.

incorrect.A: More frequent backups improve RPO somewhat, but Backup and Restore's RTO is fundamentally hours long because compute must be provisioned from scratch during recovery — no backup frequency change fixes that.
incorrect.B: Pilot Light's RTO is measured in tens of minutes, since application servers must still be provisioned and scaled up from nothing during failover — this risks exceeding the 15-minute target, unlike Warm Standby where app servers are already running, just at reduced capacity.
incorrect.D: Multi-Site Active/Active would comfortably beat the RTO/RPO targets, but it requires running full production capacity in both Regions continuously, directly violating the requirement to avoid that cost.

scenario: A company wants to insert a third-party virtual firewall appliance transparently into the traffic path between the internet and its application load balancer, so every inbound packet is inspected before reaching the application. The vendor should not need to build any AWS-specific integration, and the appliance fleet must scale automatically as traffic grows. Which load balancer should front the firewall appliances?

options.text: Application Load Balancer (ALB)
Network Load Balancer (NLB)
Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB)
Classic Load Balancer (CLB)

explanation.correct: Gateway Load Balancer is purpose-built for transparently inserting third-party virtual appliances (firewalls, IDS/IPS) inline using GENEVE encapsulation, distributing traffic across an auto-scaled appliance fleet without requiring the vendor to build any AWS-specific integration.

incorrect.A: ALB operates at Layer 7 and terminates/re-originates HTTP connections — it isn't designed for transparent, protocol-agnostic packet-level appliance insertion.
incorrect.B: NLB is Layer 4 and could front the appliances, but it lacks the GENEVE-based bump-in-the-wire semantics GWLB provides specifically for security-appliance insertion.
incorrect.D: Classic Load Balancer is a legacy offering lacking the capabilities of both ALB and NLB, and isn't used for this appliance-insertion pattern at all.

scenario: A media company has a single S3 bucket shared by 40 internal applications, each needing different permissions to different prefixes. The single bucket policy has grown past 6,000 lines and is frequently the target of accidental permission conflicts when multiple teams edit it. The company wants each application team to manage its own access rules independently, without any team being able to accidentally affect another team's access. What should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Split the single bucket into 40 separate buckets, one per application.
Create an S3 Access Point for each application, each with its own scoped policy and, where useful, restricted to a specific VPC.
Use S3 Object Lambda to enforce per-application permissions at read time.
Keep a single bucket policy, but split it into 40 separate IAM policies referencing the same bucket ARN.

explanation.correct: S3 Access Points give each application its own named access endpoint with its own scoped policy, letting teams manage access independently without one team's edits risking another's — exactly the delegated, isolated access-management problem described, without migrating any data.

incorrect.A: Splitting into 40 buckets solves isolation but requires migrating all existing data and reconfiguring every application's endpoint, and loses the benefits of a shared dataset — far more effort than Access Points require.
incorrect.C: Object Lambda transforms object content on retrieval; it isn't an access-control delegation mechanism and doesn't solve the unmanageable-single-policy problem.
incorrect.D: IAM policies attached to identities still ultimately evaluate against the same underlying bucket policy and resource, and don't eliminate the need to reason about one bucket's cross-team effects — Access Points are the AWS feature built specifically for this.

scenario: A gaming company runs a leaderboard service that must accept writes from players in both us-east-1 and eu-west-1 simultaneously, with each Region's writes visible to the other within a couple of seconds. The service needs a schema-flexible key-value model that can scale to millions of writes per second globally. Which database should they choose?

options.text: Amazon Aurora Global Database
Amazon RDS Multi-AZ
Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables
Amazon ElastiCache with cross-region replication

explanation.correct: DynamoDB Global Tables provide multi-Region, multi-active replication: every Region can accept writes simultaneously, with changes propagating to other Regions typically within seconds, and DynamoDB's schema-flexible key-value model natively scales to very high write throughput.

incorrect.A: Aurora Global Database's secondary Regions are read-only by default under one primary writer Region — it doesn't provide the same simultaneous multi-Region active-active write model DynamoDB Global Tables offers.
incorrect.B: RDS Multi-AZ is single-Region high availability, not multi-Region, and provides no multi-Region write capability at all.
incorrect.D: ElastiCache is a cache, not a durable system-of-record data store, and isn't designed to be the primary multi-region-write data store for leaderboard data.

scenario: A SaaS company exposes a public API through Amazon API Gateway to external customers on different subscription tiers. They need to limit each customer to a specific request rate based on their tier, and identify which customer is calling for billing purposes, without requiring customers to share a network location with the provider. What should they implement?

options.text: A single AWS WAF rate-based rule limiting all traffic to the API globally.
Separate VPCs per customer with security-group-based rate limiting.
API Gateway usage plans, each associated with per-customer API keys.
Route each customer's traffic through a separate Network Load Balancer with connection limits.

explanation.correct: Usage plans define per-consumer rate limits and quotas, and API keys identify which customer is calling and tie them to a specific plan — exactly the mechanism for enforcing different, per-customer request limits and attributing usage for billing.

incorrect.A: A single global WAF rate-based rule throttles all traffic together; it can't distinguish between customers on different tiers or attribute usage per customer.
incorrect.B: Customers are external SaaS consumers, not deployed inside the provider's VPC — this doesn't apply, and security groups don't perform per-customer application-level request throttling anyway.
incorrect.D: NLB connection limits operate at the network/connection level, not per-authenticated-customer request rate, and can't achieve tiered per-customer throttling tied to billing identity.

scenario: A company processes millions of short-lived IoT sensor events per day, each requiring a simple three-step workflow (validate, transform, store) that completes in under a second. Occasional duplicate processing of an event is acceptable because the storage step is idempotent, and cost per execution is the primary concern given the massive volume. Which Step Functions workflow type should they use?

options.text: Standard workflow
Express workflow
A single Lambda function with no Step Functions at all
Standard workflow with a shorter execution timeout configured

explanation.correct: Express workflows are priced by execution count and duration/memory rather than per state transition, making them dramatically cheaper at this volume, and they guarantee only at-least-once execution — acceptable here since the storage step is idempotent — well within their 5-minute cap.

incorrect.A: Standard workflows are priced per state transition, which becomes expensive at millions of executions a day for a multi-step workflow, and its exactly-once guarantee is unneeded overhead given the idempotent storage step.
incorrect.C: A single Lambda function could technically run this logic, but loses the built-in state visualization, retry, and error handling Step Functions provides for a defined multi-step workflow — the exam expects Step Functions for a described multi-step process.
incorrect.D: Shortening a Standard workflow's timeout doesn't change its per-state-transition pricing model, so it doesn't address the cost problem at this volume.

scenario: A video streaming company wants to serve premium content through CloudFront only to logged-in, paying subscribers, blocking free-tier users even if they discover a CloudFront URL directly. Each subscriber only ever needs access to the handful of videos they've individually purchased. What is the best mechanism?

options.text: CloudFront signed cookies
CloudFront signed URLs
A public S3 bucket policy allowing GetObject to any authenticated AWS user
An AWS WAF geo-blocking rule

explanation.correct: Signed URLs grant time-limited access to one specific file at a time, which fits a subscriber who only needs access to a handful of individually purchased videos — the minimal-blast-radius choice for per-object entitlements.

incorrect.A: Signed cookies are the better fit when a viewer needs access to many files under one grant (e.g. an entire catalog) without re-signing each URL — here, subscribers need only a handful of specific videos, which signed URLs handle more precisely.
incorrect.C: A policy granting access to any authenticated AWS user would require every viewer to hold an AWS IAM identity, which end consumers of a streaming service don't have — this isn't how consumer content restriction works.
incorrect.D: Geo-blocking restricts by location, not by subscription or payment status, and doesn't address the actual requirement.

scenario: A financial services company runs a tightly-coupled computational fluid dynamics simulation across 50 EC2 instances that constantly exchange data with each other, and the primary bottleneck is inter-instance network latency. Which placement strategy should they use?

options.text: Spread placement group
Partition placement group
Cluster placement group
No placement group; rely on Auto Scaling across multiple Availability Zones

explanation.correct: Cluster placement groups pack instances physically close together within a single Availability Zone specifically to minimize inter-instance network latency — exactly the tightly-coupled HPC use case described.

incorrect.A: Spread placement groups intentionally place instances on distinct underlying hardware to minimize simultaneous failure risk, which increases inter-instance latency — the opposite of what's needed here.
incorrect.B: Partition placement groups isolate groups of instances from each other for fault isolation (used by distributed systems like Hadoop/Cassandra) — they don't focus on minimizing latency between every instance.
incorrect.D: Spreading instances across multiple AZs would significantly increase inter-instance latency from inter-AZ network hops, working directly against the stated bottleneck.

scenario: An application running on EC2 instances in a private subnet reads and writes large volumes of data to an S3 bucket in the same Region. The company wants to avoid all data-transfer and per-hour endpoint charges for this traffic while keeping it off the public internet entirely. What should they configure?

options.text: A NAT Gateway in a public subnet, with a route from the private subnet
An Interface VPC endpoint for S3
A Gateway VPC endpoint for S3
An AWS PrivateLink connection to a partner service

explanation.correct: Gateway endpoints for S3 (and DynamoDB) carry no hourly or per-GB charge and keep traffic entirely on AWS's network via a route table entry — exactly matching the requirement to avoid all charges while staying off the public internet.

incorrect.A: A NAT Gateway would route traffic out to S3's public endpoint over the internet path and incurs its own hourly plus per-GB data-processing charges — it fails both the cost and off-internet requirements.
incorrect.B: Interface endpoints keep traffic private but are ENI-based and incur hourly plus per-GB charges — Gateway endpoints are the free option specifically for S3 and DynamoDB.
incorrect.D: PrivateLink is the general mechanism behind interface endpoints to partner/custom services — unnecessary and not free, when a Gateway endpoint already solves this exact S3 case at no cost.

scenario: During a Well-Architected Framework review, a team finds that a stable, predictable production workload has run on On-Demand EC2 pricing for two years with no Reserved Instances or Savings Plans in place, despite consistent, unchanging usage — resulting in significantly higher spend than necessary with no corresponding benefit. Which pillar does this finding primarily relate to?

options.text: Reliability
Performance Efficiency
Cost Optimization
Operational Excellence

explanation.correct: Failing to use commitment-based discounts (Reserved Instances/Savings Plans) for stable, predictable usage is a pure spend-avoidance issue with no complexity or performance dimension — squarely a Cost Optimization pillar finding.

incorrect.A: Reliability concerns recovering from failures and meeting demand — this finding is about unnecessary spend, not failure recovery.
incorrect.B: Performance Efficiency is about matching resource type/sizing to workload needs — this finding involves no resource-type or sizing issue, purely a pricing-model choice.
incorrect.D: Operational Excellence concerns running, monitoring, and improving operational processes — this finding is a purchasing decision, not a process gap.

scenario: A company wants to be automatically alerted whenever spending on any AWS service deviates unexpectedly from its normal historical pattern, without manually defining specific dollar thresholds for every service in advance, since new services are added to their environment regularly. Which tool should they use?

options.text: AWS Budgets
AWS Cost Explorer
AWS Cost Anomaly Detection
AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR)

explanation.correct: Cost Anomaly Detection uses machine learning to learn each service's normal spending pattern automatically and alerts on unexpected deviations, with no need to manually predefine thresholds per service — including new services added later.

incorrect.A: Budgets requires manually defining a specific threshold per budget; it doesn't automatically adapt to what's 'normal' or automatically cover newly added services without configuration.
incorrect.B: Cost Explorer is retrospective, manual analysis — someone has to go look for anomalies; it doesn't proactively alert on its own.
incorrect.D: CUR is raw line-item billing data meant for custom analysis, not an alerting mechanism at all.

scenario: A company's finance team purchased a large Compute Savings Plan in the Organization's management account expecting it to reduce costs across all member accounts. Two months later they notice one specific member account's EC2 costs remain at full On-Demand rates while every other account shows the expected discount. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Savings Plans can only ever apply to the account that purchased them, and the finance team misunderstood how they work.
That specific member account has disabled Savings Plan sharing for itself, opting out of Organization-wide sharing.
Compute Savings Plans do not apply to EC2 usage at all, only to Fargate and Lambda.
The Savings Plan has already been fully consumed by other accounts and no capacity remains.

explanation.correct: Savings Plans and RIs are shared org-wide by default via consolidated billing, but an individual member account can opt out of receiving shared benefit — this is the standard explanation for one account seeing full On-Demand rates while every other account gets the discount.

incorrect.A: Savings Plans and RIs are shared across an Organization by default — the opposite of this claim — which is the common misconception this option is testing.
incorrect.C: Compute Savings Plans do apply to EC2 (as well as Fargate and Lambda) — this option states something false about the service.
incorrect.D: Savings Plans provide a discount on usage up to a committed spend rate rather than a finite consumable 'capacity'; even if the commitment were fully applied elsewhere, the excluded account would still get its own On-Demand rate for its usage rather than zero discount specifically because others 'used it up.'

scenario: A company has deployed AWS Config rules individually across each of its 30 AWS accounts to check for a specific compliance standard. Keeping the rules consistent as the standard evolves has become a significant manual burden, and when a non-compliant resource is found, an engineer must manually intervene to fix it every time. What should a solutions architect recommend to reduce this operational burden?

options.text: Migrate all Config rules to Amazon EventBridge rules instead.
Package the Config rules into a conformance pack deployed across the Organization, with SSM Automation documents attached for auto-remediation.
Replace AWS Config entirely with a third-party compliance scanning tool.
Consolidate all 30 accounts into a single account to simplify rule management.

explanation.correct: Conformance packs bundle and version Config rules for consistent, one-step Organization-wide deployment, and attaching SSM Automation documents enables automatic remediation without manual intervention — directly addressing both stated pain points.

incorrect.A: EventBridge is not a compliance-rule engine; migrating to it addresses neither rule consistency nor auto-remediation.
incorrect.C: Replacing Config entirely is a far larger, unnecessary change when Config's own conformance pack and remediation features already solve the exact problem described.
incorrect.D: Consolidating 30 accounts into one is an extreme, high-risk restructuring that eliminates the security and blast-radius benefits of multi-account separation — not a reasonable response to a rule-management problem.

scenario: A healthcare company must retain patient record backups for 7 years under a regulatory requirement. A recent internal audit flagged a risk: a compromised administrator credential could currently delete these backups before their retention period expires. The company needs this to be provably impossible, even for their own administrators, without waiting for a new audit cycle. What should they implement?

options.text: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) on all administrator accounts.
AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode.
AWS Backup Vault Lock in governance mode.
A service control policy (SCP) denying backup:DeleteRecoveryPoint for all users.

explanation.correct: Compliance mode makes a Vault Lock policy irreversible, even for the account root user or AWS itself, providing the 'provably impossible, even for our own administrators' guarantee the audit requires.

incorrect.A: MFA reduces the risk of credential compromise but doesn't make deletion provably impossible for a legitimate or compromised-but-authenticated administrator — it's a preventive access control, not an enforcement guarantee on the backups themselves.
incorrect.C: Governance mode still allows sufficiently privileged users to remove or override the lock, so it doesn't provide the same irreversible guarantee compliance mode does.
incorrect.D: An SCP denying delete actions could, in principle, still be modified or removed by someone with sufficient Organizations-level permissions — it isn't the purpose-built, irreversible compliance guarantee Vault Lock's compliance mode specifically provides.

scenario: An operations team wants a detailed, data-driven recommendation for the ideal EC2 instance type and size for each of 200 running instances, based on actual historical CPU, memory, and network utilization patterns over the past two weeks. Which service should they use?

options.text: AWS Trusted Advisor
AWS Compute Optimizer
Amazon CloudWatch dashboards
AWS Config

explanation.correct: Compute Optimizer is the purpose-built, ML-driven rightsizing recommendation engine that analyzes CPU, memory, and network utilization history to recommend specific instance types and sizes.

incorrect.A: Trusted Advisor provides broader best-practice checks, including some cost checks, but not the same depth of per-instance utilization-driven rightsizing analysis, and its fuller check set is gated by support plan tier.
incorrect.C: CloudWatch dashboards expose the raw metrics but require manual analysis and decision-making — there's no automated recommendation engine behind them.
incorrect.D: AWS Config checks resource configuration against compliance rules, not performance or utilization-based sizing recommendations.

scenario: A company's microservices application — composed of API Gateway, several Lambda functions, and a downstream DynamoDB table — has recently started experiencing intermittent high latency for end users, but the team cannot determine which specific service in the request chain is responsible. Which service should they use to pinpoint the bottleneck?

options.text: Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights
AWS X-Ray
Amazon CloudWatch Alarms
AWS CloudTrail

explanation.correct: X-Ray traces individual requests end-to-end across the full microservices chain and visualizes exactly where time is spent via a service map — precisely what's needed to isolate which specific component is causing the latency.

incorrect.A: Logs Insights can query each service's logs individually, but doesn't automatically correlate a single request's journey across multiple services the way X-Ray's distributed tracing does.
incorrect.C: CloudWatch Alarms only notify when a metric crosses a threshold; they don't diagnose where in a request chain the latency originates.
incorrect.D: CloudTrail records API management-plane activity — who changed what — not application request latency or tracing, and is unrelated to this troubleshooting need.

scenario: A company runs a 15-year-old on-premises inventory management application built on a discontinued vendor platform that is no longer actively maintained or supported. An equivalent, fully-featured cloud-based SaaS inventory management product already exists on the market, meeting all current requirements at a lower total cost than maintaining or re-architecting the legacy application. Which of the 6 R's migration strategies best fits this situation?

options.text: Rehost
Replatform
Repurchase
Refactor

explanation.correct: Repurchase means switching to a different product, typically an existing SaaS replacement, which is exactly what's described — a SaaS product that meets the need better and cheaper than migrating or rebuilding the legacy application at all.

incorrect.A: Rehost ('lift and shift') would move the legacy, unsupported application as-is to AWS, but the available SaaS alternative is a better fit than continuing to run unsupported legacy software anywhere, even in the cloud.
incorrect.B: Replatform makes targeted optimizations to the existing application (such as swapping its database) — but the application runs on a discontinued, unmaintained platform, making incremental optimization impractical.
incorrect.D: Refactor means re-architecting the application to be cloud-native — a much larger investment than needed when an existing SaaS product already solves the problem outright.

scenario: A company needs to migrate its production database from on-premises Oracle to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, including all custom stored procedures and triggers, with minimal application downtime during cutover. What should they use?

options.text: AWS DMS alone, to migrate schema, code, and data all in one step.
AWS SCT to convert schema and code first, then AWS DMS to perform ongoing data replication and final cutover.
AWS DataSync to copy the database files directly to Aurora.
Export the Oracle database to CSV files and import them into Aurora PostgreSQL using the COPY command.

explanation.correct: This is the standard heterogeneous migration pairing: SCT converts schema and code — including stored procedures and triggers that differ between source and target engines — while DMS performs continuous change-data-capture replication for a minimal-downtime cutover.

incorrect.A: DMS migrates data only, not schema or code logic like stored procedures and triggers; for heterogeneous migrations between different database engines it must be paired with SCT first.
incorrect.C: DataSync is for file and object data transfer (e.g. NFS/SMB to S3/EFS), not database engine migration with schema conversion — the wrong tool entirely for this use case.
incorrect.D: A manual CSV export/import loses all stored procedures and triggers, which aren't captured in a data-only export, and would require significant downtime during the full export/import window — failing both stated requirements.

scenario: A media company runs a containerized video transcoding batch job on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate, processing a queue of videos throughout the day. Individual transcoding jobs can safely restart from the beginning if interrupted, and the company wants to reduce compute costs for this workload as much as possible without changing container images or application code. What should they do?

options.text: Switch the ECS service to use the EC2 launch type instead of Fargate.
Configure the ECS service to use a Fargate Spot capacity provider strategy alongside standard Fargate.
Move the workload to AWS Lambda instead.
Purchase a Compute Savings Plan committing to 3 years of steady Fargate usage.

explanation.correct: Fargate Spot offers up to roughly a 70% discount for interruptible workloads like this restart-tolerant transcoding job, without any change to container images or code, and a capacity provider strategy can blend Spot with standard Fargate for resilience.

incorrect.A: Switching to EC2 launch type reintroduces server and cluster management that Fargate was chosen to avoid, and doesn't inherently guarantee a lower cost than Fargate Spot for this workload.
incorrect.C: Moving to Lambda would require re-architecting the application around Lambda's execution model and limits (e.g. a 15-minute maximum duration), violating the 'without changing application code' requirement, and video transcoding jobs often exceed Lambda's constraints.
incorrect.D: A Savings Plan requires a long-term steady-usage commitment and offers a smaller discount than Spot for a workload that is explicitly interruptible and restart-tolerant — Spot is the better fit given the stated fault tolerance.

scenario: A research institution needs to migrate 2 petabytes of existing data from an on-premises data center to Amazon S3. Their available internet connection provides 100 Mbps of usable bandwidth, and calculations show that transferring the full dataset over this connection would take several months. What should they use instead?

options.text: AWS DataSync over the existing internet connection.
AWS Snowball Edge devices (or AWS Snowmobile, depending on final data volume assessment).
Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration.
AWS Direct Connect with a new 1 Gbps dedicated connection.

explanation.correct: When transferring data over the network would take weeks or months, a physical Snow Family device is the answer; at petabyte scale, a fleet of Snowball Edge devices (or, historically, Snowmobile at exabyte scale) moves the data far faster by physically shipping storage rather than sending it over a constrained link.

incorrect.A: DataSync accelerates transfers over an existing network connection but is still bound by that connection's bandwidth — it doesn't solve a fundamental 'the pipe is too small for this volume in a reasonable time' problem.
incorrect.C: S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds transfers by routing through CloudFront edge locations, but still depends on the underlying 100 Mbps connection — it doesn't fundamentally change a months-long timeline.
incorrect.D: Provisioning a new Direct Connect connection takes significant lead time (often weeks) to establish and is a recurring infrastructure commitment — a heavier, slower-to-provision solution than shipping a Snow device for a one-time bulk transfer.

scenario: A development team wants to define their infrastructure as code, but finds hand-writing repetitive CloudFormation YAML for dozens of near-identical microservice stacks time-consuming and error-prone. They would prefer to use loops, conditionals, and reusable functions in a programming language the team already knows (TypeScript) to generate that infrastructure, while still retaining CloudFormation's stack management, rollback, and drift detection underneath. What should they use?

options.text: AWS OpsWorks
AWS CDK
AWS Elastic Beanstalk
Terraform

explanation.correct: CDK lets teams define infrastructure in TypeScript (or other general-purpose languages) using full programming constructs — loops, conditionals, reusable constructs — synthesizing down to standard CloudFormation templates, so it still gets CloudFormation's own stack management, rollback, and drift detection.

incorrect.A: OpsWorks is a configuration management service (Chef/Puppet-based), not an infrastructure-as-code templating tool matching this need.
incorrect.C: Elastic Beanstalk is a PaaS for deploying applications, not a general infrastructure-as-code authoring tool with programming-language constructs.
incorrect.D: Terraform could achieve similar programmatic IaC goals, but it isn't natively CloudFormation-based — it uses its own state file and engine, not CloudFormation stacks — while the requirement is specifically to retain CloudFormation's own stack management underneath, which only CDK provides.

scenario: A new global news publishing platform needs a primary read-write Region (us-east-1) plus low-latency read access for users in ap-southeast-1 and eu-west-1, with typical replication lag under 1 second, and the ability to promote a secondary Region to full read-write within about a minute if the primary Region fails — using a standard MySQL-compatible relational engine. Which should they use?

options.text: Amazon RDS for MySQL with cross-region read replicas
Amazon Aurora MySQL-Compatible Global Database
Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables, redesigning the schema from relational to NoSQL
An Aurora MySQL Multi-AZ cluster, with ongoing replication to other Regions handled by AWS DMS replication tasks

explanation.correct: Aurora Global Database replicates at the storage layer with typical lag under 1 second — well below standard logical replication — and its managed failover is purpose-built to promote a secondary Region to full read-write in about a minute, all while keeping a standard MySQL-compatible relational engine.

incorrect.A: RDS cross-region read replicas use MySQL binlog-based logical replication, which typically has higher and more variable lag than Aurora Global Database's storage-level replication, and manual promotion isn't optimized for a roughly one-minute RTO.
incorrect.C: Redesigning the schema from relational to NoSQL is a far larger effort than needed when Aurora Global Database already meets the relational and low-latency global-read requirements without any data model change.
incorrect.D: DMS is a migration and one-off/ongoing replication tool, not a purpose-built multi-region high-availability solution — it lacks Aurora Global Database's managed failover tooling and sub-second replication lag guarantee.

scenario:
A company is designing a new CI/CD pipeline for an application spanning three separate AWS accounts (Dev, Test, Prod) under one Organization for isolation. Requirements:

- The pipeline must build once and promote the same immutable artifact through Dev, Test, and Prod, never rebuilding at each stage.
- Deploying to the Prod account must not require long-lived IAM credentials for the Prod account to be stored in the CI/CD tooling account.
- A manual approval gate must exist before deployment to Prod.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy entirely separate CodePipeline instances in each of the three accounts, each independently pulling source and rebuilding from scratch.

Run a single CodePipeline in a central tooling account; use CodeBuild to produce one build artifact stored in S3/ECR, then use cross-account IAM roles via CodePipeline's cross-account action configuration to deploy that same artifact to Test and Prod, with a manual approval action gating the Prod stage.
Store a single set of long-lived IAM access keys for each of the three accounts as pipeline secrets, using them to authenticate deployment actions to each account.
Use three independent CI workflows, one per account, each triggered independently on every commit.

explanation.correct: One pipeline building a single artifact and promoting it through cross-account IAM roles (assumed via CodePipeline's native cross-account action support, requiring no stored long-lived credentials) plus a native manual approval action before Prod satisfies all three requirements directly.

incorrect.A: Rebuilding independently in each account violates 'build once, promote the same artifact' and risks environment drift between what was tested and what actually gets deployed to Prod.
incorrect.C: Long-lived IAM access keys stored as pipeline secrets directly violate the requirement to avoid long-lived credentials for Prod, and carry ongoing credential-leak risk.
incorrect.D: Three independently triggered workflows can't guarantee the same artifact is promoted unchanged across accounts, and provide no single controlled approval gate before Prod.

scenario: A company is building a new order-processing system where orders for a given customer must be processed in the exact order they were placed. Expected peak load is roughly 2,000 orders per second across all customers combined. Multiple independent downstream systems (billing, fulfillment, analytics) each need to process every order, and if any one of them has a bug, that team needs the ability to independently replay and reprocess the last 24 hours of order events in their original order, without affecting the other downstream systems. Which should they choose?

options.text: An SQS Standard queue
An SQS FIFO queue
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, using customer ID as the partition key, with a 24-hour retention period
An SNS topic fanning out to one SQS queue per downstream system

explanation.correct: Kinesis Data Streams guarantees ordering within a partition key (customer ID), scales well beyond SQS's throughput ceiling via shards, and — critically — retains data for a configurable window so each independent consumer can replay and reprocess events from any point in that window on its own, without affecting other consumers. That replay capability is the deciding requirement here, and neither SQS option provides it.

incorrect.A: SQS Standard doesn't guarantee ordering at all, and once a message is deleted after processing, it's gone — there's no way to replay it later.
incorrect.B: SQS FIFO guarantees ordering per message group and exactly-once processing, but has no replay capability: once a message is successfully processed and deleted, it cannot be reprocessed, failing the 'replay the last 24 hours' requirement.
incorrect.D: Fanning out through SNS to per-system SQS queues still inherits SQS's lack of retention-based replay once messages are consumed and deleted, and a standard SNS topic doesn't guarantee ordering the way a Kinesis partition key does.

scenario: A company is launching a new real-time multiplayer game backend that communicates with clients over UDP for gameplay traffic. It needs consistent low latency by routing each player to the closest healthy regional endpoint, plus fast failover (in seconds) if a Region becomes unhealthy. The traffic is not HTTP/HTTPS and cannot be cached. Which service should front this traffic?

options.text: Amazon CloudFront
AWS Global Accelerator
Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing alone
An Application Load Balancer with cross-zone load balancing enabled

explanation.correct: Global Accelerator operates at the network layer over both TCP and UDP, using static Anycast IPs to route each client to the closest healthy regional endpoint with fast, health-check-driven failover — independent of HTTP and well suited to non-cacheable, real-time gameplay traffic.

incorrect.A: CloudFront is an HTTP(S) content-delivery and caching service; it doesn't support arbitrary UDP traffic or non-cacheable real-time gameplay data.
incorrect.C: Route 53 latency-based routing directs DNS resolution to the closest Region, but failover depends on DNS TTL expiry and client re-resolution, which is far slower than Global Accelerator's near-instant Anycast-based failover.
incorrect.D: An ALB operates within a single Region at Layer 7 (HTTP) — it provides neither multi-Region routing nor UDP support.

scenario: A company is building a new centralized data lake on S3 that will be queried by dozens of analyst teams via Athena and Redshift Spectrum. Each team should only see specific tables, and in some cases only specific columns or rows within a table (for example, finance analysts can see salary columns but no other team can), with access centrally managed and audited in one place rather than through per-team S3 bucket policies. What should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Create a separate S3 bucket per team, each with its own bucket policy limiting access to that team's data.
Use AWS Lake Formation to centrally define and enforce table-, column-, and row-level permissions across all teams querying the shared data lake.
Encrypt sensitive columns with separate per-team KMS keys, granting each team decrypt access only to their own columns' key.
Rely solely on IAM policies applied directly to the underlying S3 objects, with a separate policy per team per table.

explanation.correct: Lake Formation is purpose-built for centralized, fine-grained (table, column, and row-level) permission management across a shared data lake queried through Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and Glue, with centralized auditing — without duplicating data or infrastructure per team.

incorrect.A: Separate buckets per team fragment the centralized data-lake model, add data duplication and synchronization overhead, and still can't provide column- or row-level granularity within a shared table.
incorrect.C: Per-team KMS keys can approximate column-level protection but become unwieldy at scale, provide no row-level filtering, and lack the centralized query-time enforcement and auditing Lake Formation gives natively.
incorrect.D: S3-object-level IAM policies operate at object/prefix granularity, not table, column, or row granularity within a shared table — they don't achieve the fine-grained requirement described.

scenario: A company is building a new machine learning training pipeline that needs a shared, POSIX-compliant file system accessible concurrently from hundreds of EC2 GPU instances, with sub-millisecond latencies and throughput scaling into the hundreds of GB/s to keep the GPUs fed with training data, with the data sourced from and written back to S3 for durability. Which storage service should they use?

options.text: Amazon EFS
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
Amazon FSx for Lustre
An Amazon EBS Multi-Attach volume shared across all instances

explanation.correct: FSx for Lustre is purpose-built for HPC/ML workloads that need very high throughput (hundreds of GB/s) and sub-millisecond latencies, and it natively integrates with S3 to lazily load training data in and write results back out.

incorrect.A: EFS is POSIX-compliant and scales to thousands of concurrent connections, but its latency and per-client throughput profile targets general-purpose shared file workloads, not the very high-throughput performance tier FSx for Lustre specifically targets.
incorrect.B: FSx for Windows File Server serves SMB-based, Active-Directory-integrated Windows workloads — not a POSIX Linux HPC/ML use case, and not optimized for this performance tier.
incorrect.D: EBS Multi-Attach lets a small number of Nitro instances attach the same block volume, but it's a block device, not a shared file system, and isn't designed for hundreds of concurrently mounted GPU instances with S3 integration.
